hero.subtitle: The next generation Internet Protocol — 128-bit addresses for a connected world

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6) is the successor to IPv4 (RFC 791), designed to address the exhaustion of the 32-bit IPv4 address space. IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, providing approximately 3.4 × 1038 unique addresses — enough for every grain of sand on Earth to have its own address.

IPv6 was first specified in RFC 2460 (1998) and updated by this RFC (8200) in 2017, which was promoted to Internet Standard. The transition from IPv4 to IPv6 is one of the longest infrastructure migrations in computing history.

Beyond the larger address space, IPv6 introduces a simplified header format, eliminates the need for NAT, mandates IPsec support, and provides built-in support for mobility and autoconfiguration.

VersionInternet Protocol version number: 64 bits
Traffic ClassDifferentiated services (DSCP) and ECN bits8 bits
Flow LabelLabels packets belonging to a flow for QoS handling20 bits
Payload LengthLength of the payload in bytes (after the 40-byte header)16 bits
Next HeaderIdentifies the type of header following the IPv6 header (e.g., TCP = 6, UDP = 17)8 bits
Hop LimitDecremented by 1 at each forwarding node; packet discarded when 0 (replaces IPv4 TTL)8 bits
Source Address128-bit address of the originator128 bits
Destination Address128-bit address of the intended recipient128 bits

sections.title: Improvements over IPv4
sections.content:
IPv6 was designed to fix the shortcomings of IPv4 while simplifying router processing:

Feature
IPv4 (RFC 791)
IPv6 (RFC 8200)
Address Size
32 bits (~4.3 billion)
128 bits (~3.4 × 10³⁸)
Header Size
20–60 bytes (variable)
40 bytes (fixed)
Fragmentation
By routers or sender
By sender only
Header Checksum
Yes (recomputed at each hop)
Removed (relies on link-layer and transport checksums)
NAT Required?
Common (address scarcity)
No (abundant addresses)
Autoconfiguration
DHCP only
SLAAC + DHCPv6

By removing the header checksum and making the header fixed-length, IPv6 significantly reduces per-packet processing at routers, enabling faster forwarding in hardware.

sections.title: Extension Headers
sections.content:
IPv6 replaces IPv4's variable-length options with a chain of extension headers, each identified by the Next Header field of the preceding header:

0Hop-by-Hop Options — processed by every node along the path
43Routing — specifies intermediate nodes to visit (source routing)
44Fragment — contains fragmentation and reassembly information
50Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) — encryption and authentication
51Authentication Header (AH) — integrity and authentication
60Destination Options — processed only by the destination node

Extension headers are only examined by the destination node (with the exception of Hop-by-Hop Options), making router processing more efficient. They form a linked list, with each header's Next Header field pointing to the next.

sections.title: Addressing
sections.content:
IPv6 addresses are 128 bits long, written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons:

IPv6 Address Notation
Full:       2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001
Compressed: 2001:db8::1
Loopback:   ::1
Link-local: fe80::1%eth0
Unicast
Identifies a single interface. Global unicast addresses (2000::/3) are routable on the public Internet. Link-local addresses (fe80::/10) are used for communication on a single link.
Multicast
Identifies a group of interfaces (ff00::/8). IPv6 replaces IPv4 broadcast with multicast — there is no broadcast address in IPv6.
Anycast
Assigned to multiple interfaces; packets are delivered to the nearest one (by routing metric). Used for service discovery and load distribution.
Address Length128 bits (16 bytes)
Total Addresses~3.4 × 10³⁸
EtherType0x86DD
Header Size40 bytes (fixed)
